title: How do most people get their visual assets?
author: Adventurous_Push6483
selftext:
Not doing market research, just curious about how people are obtaining their assets. Particularly visual assets (e.g, textures including procedural, models, art, etc, excluding things like music, voice, code, etc). Assuming AI coding.

\- Creates majority of assets through traditional ways (Photoshop/clip studio, blender hard modeling, etc)

\- Uses majority stock/asset packs.

\- Uses generative AI/stock objects for pre-vis, then traditionally creates assets (e.g, generate a reference character with GPT image 2 then sculpt character).

\- Uses mostly generative AI/agents to create assets.

comments.author: MistakeForsaken6653
comments.body:
sketchfab is a good place for some free textures.  for models I usually make those myself but have used the unity asset store or [itch.io](http://itch.io) to find some free placeholders until the ones I make are done.  I then will often use mixamo to rig those models and animate them.

for  low poly games are willing to spend money synty has a lot of good packs but they will set you back around 150.00.  

In my first game I did use quite a bit of gen ai 2d pixel art but have stopped doing that as that did come back to bite me since people really hate seeing that in their games.

replies.author: Nez_Coupe
replies.body:
I’ve been trying to nail down a good process to get the 2d “pixel art” to be less noisy and dirty looking from genAI and I think I’m getting close. I’ll usually downsample 2x or 3x with lanczos and a despeckle filter, then quantize down to 32 colors, or 48 if there are a lot of hues, then I’ll reprocess the image with a box average and another 2x downsample, which usually gets me down to where I need to be. If there’s still speckling I’ll run the despeckle again on the second process. 

I know very little about image processing but it’s getting me close.

replies.author: Pokeperson5
replies.body: I've been having the exact same problem. Single pixel art images look good, but as soon as you go to animations it just becomes a noisy mess. No matter how much post processing I use, I just can't get the quality I want.

comments.author: saviorofGOAT
comments.body:
You can always check for people down for rev share or just find a cheap artist to start. There's plenty for $10 & under on fiverr just make sure theyrr not using ai or youre wasting your money. In the meantime you can use programmer art in the meantime or just random assets off itch.

I would strongly recommend against AI Gen assets if for no other reason, they are TERRIBLE for branding in the current environment unless you can really push them into not looking anything like ai while somehow making them cohesive. If you still take this route try to find someone who knows what they are looking for to tell you if it still looks like ai. You won't know what you're not seeing.

And yes, mspaint doodles are better for branding and marketing your game than Genai right now. At least there's not a massive amount of people who will auto-hate you for using them and people will assume you're not keeping them forever.

Slay the spire beta art looked like it was made by a literal child and look how that game turned out.

GL

comments.author: ZymzAlchemy
comments.body:
I created my own model checkpoints trained on my art style.   
I then feed my sketches to the generator and have it spit out polished concepts.   
I resketch the individual assets for the concepts as base sprites with proper perspective and orientation which is something the generator sucks at. And then feed them into the generator for paint and color.   
Those sprites are then used as a base to have the LLM generate animated sprite sheets for each animation.   
Sprite sheets are easily processed by your agent and wired into your project.   
I have documents that guide the art styles, prompting, architecture and the like so the agent has a large amount of context to guardrail against disaster.   
Assets and sheets are given a final polish with GIMP so they snap.   
Good luck and keep creating.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: AI for refs which I then use traditional poly modeling / painting workflows to bring to life. I don't have the time to be F'ed trying to think up exactly how every character feature should look in practice, and didn't want all my characters to end up looking the same (Hi Skyrim), so having AI which can pump out ideas en masse to  weed out or  proof is great. It might not be doing the actual asset creation, but it gives me WAYYY more time to do that part (which is more enjoyable anyway, at least for me.)

comments.body: I haven't done many 3d assets with the new models, but the ones that I did do I had a 2d mock-up done with Gemini or chatgpt, then I had Meshi AI make a 3d version of it. comments.author: Kashmakers
comments.body:
I'm an artist, I draw everything myself.

The issue with AI generated art is mostly the inconsistency of it, and people never really having an art direction or style that ties it all together. But you can definitely get AI to render something close to the same style, you just have to do your research and find out which style that is.

Pixel art still isn't there yet in my opinion, it is never consistent with pixel art unless you give it control of Aseprite or something.

There's plenty of asset packs available to purchase though. And if you need something specific, just feed your current assets into the AI and tell it to stick close to the style and render something new. Editing may be required.

comments.author: HaMMeReD
comments.body:
For [nubu3d.com](http://nubu3d.com) where I am going to start taking pet photos and making prints, I use reference photos -> contact sheet (4-up) which I split into 4 images (tlrb) and then send to Meshy for generation, review the untextured generation. It can be anywhere from downright terrible to nearly perfect. Then once that is good I use that to generate a textured mesh w/PBR layers and such.

(and from there I do printer prep for a color print).

Depending on the game, I'd do similar for AI driven assets.

comments.author: Seven-Prime
comments.body:
I spent some time to build up an asset pipeline starting from a world bible, then an art bible. Started at block out level surfaces so I could have something to work with. Expanded that to include first pass of flora. But had all the flora planned out before I started. Then spent some cycles authoring everything.

The point is that I had a methodical way so that assets all start out as metadata and text descriptions.

comments.author: ferrx
comments.body:
I like Meshy for 3d models and AutoSprite for 2d, especially 2d animation. 

If you’re willing to build your own animations, meshy is great, but it really lacks anything useful beyond static models. Their animation library is wonky and limited.  

As for autosprite, their selling point is 2d animation. They let you storyboard the clip, so once you have some poses, you can let it fill in the blanks pretty well. 

All of these tools can be frustrating half the time, generating unusables. It will improve.
